clue.text: Tailed off in descant

indicators.note: something gone off has turned bad or is off course, so the word before it is put out of its proper order

parts.note: taken as written: six letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A singer's high harmony line trails away into silence.
explanation.walkthrough: A descant is a high melody over a hymn, but as a verb, to descant is to talk at length on a subject.
explanation.definitionFit: Both verbs mean to speak or write at great length, as in dilating or descanting upon a favourite topic.

clue.text: The listener Keats in deep purple?

definitions.text: The listener Keats in deep purple?

parts.note: surface: the poet sitting and listening, as he does to the bird in his nightingale ode
setter's reading: the opening word of the ode's stanza where the poet listens in the dusk, a word meaning in the dark

explanation.walkthrough: Keats's Ode to a Nightingale has 'Darkling I listen'; deep purple stands for the gathering dark in which he hears the bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb means in the dark or at dusk, which is the shadowy purple setting where the poet hears the singing bird.

clue.text: By definition, these pigs can't fly!

definitions.text: By definition, these pigs can't fly!

parts.note: surface: the old joke that pigs might fly
setter's reading: the breed's name itself says they keep to the ground and run

explanation.walkthrough: Landrace is a breed of pig; split as LAND RACE, the name describes a contest on the ground, not in the air.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a well-known white breed of domestic swine, whose name read literally suggests running on earth rather than flying.

clue.text: She hooted as I turned

indicators.note: something turned is twisted round out of its original order, so the letters before it are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written: nine letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A woman hoots with laughter as someone turns away.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is a woman's given name, and 'She' stands for any female person, so a girl's name fits.

clue.text: The case of a not very striking poet?

parts.note: a scab is a worker who refuses to join a strike
a bard is a poet

explanation.surface: A dull poet's work is put on trial as a legal case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not very striking' sounds like 'unimpressive', but it means someone who will not go on strike.
explanation.definitionFit: A sword or dagger is kept in a sheath of leather or metal, so this is literally the blade's case.

clue.text: Catch the painter getting oil from it

parts.note: to cop is to catch
RA, Royal Academician, is the crossword's usual painter

explanation.surface: An artist is caught while fetching oil for his paints.
explanation.definitionFit: Dried coconut kernel is pressed to extract coconut oil, so it is the source from which that oil is obtained.

clue.text: "The blue — its eternal bosom" (Keats)

parts.note: surface: a line of verse with a word left out
setter's reading: supply the missing word from the poet's sonnet To Homer

explanation.walkthrough: In Keats's sonnet To Homer the sky is uncovered for the blind poet: 'the blue / Bared its eternal bosom'.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing verb means uncovered or laid open, which is what the sky does to its bosom in the sonnet.

clue.text: A siren all got up

indicators.note: read as 'all over the place', telling the solver that the letters before it are scattered

parts.note: taken as written: six letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A seductive woman is all dressed up for the evening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'All got up' reads as dressed up; the definition is the plain past participle of rising, and the indicator role of 'all' is loose.
explanation.definitionFit: Having stood or risen from bed, a person has gotten to their feet, the past participle of the verb rise.

clue.text: Do leave off!

parts.note: surface: an exasperated plea to stop pestering
setter's reading: the emphatic 'do' makes it a formal command to cease

explanation.definitionFit: The formal verb means to cease or stop an action, exactly the order given in the exasperated exclamation.

clue.text: Bookie's man a Welsher

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the messenger who carries bets to a bookmaker
second meaning: one who runs off without paying what he owes

explanation.walkthrough: A welsher is someone who fails to pay a bet; the capital W tempts you to look for a Welshman.
explanation.definitionFit: The bookmaker's messenger carries bets, and someone who absconds instead of paying is one who flees from debts.

clue.text: Order to elevate pigtails leads to rë-proaches

parts.note: the command 'up!' tells something to rise
pigtails are plaits of hair

explanation.surface: Telling a girl to put her pigtails up brings complaints.
explanation.definitionFit: To scold or find fault with someone sharply is to reproach them, and the third-person verb forms match.

clue.text: Come here by way of a plank?

definitions.text: Come here by way of a plank?

parts.note: surface: crossing over on a timber, as pirates' victims were made to walk one
setter's reading: the invitation to step onto a ship by its gangplank

explanation.definitionFit: Passengers join a vessel by walking up the gangway, and 'come' plus this word is the invitation to embark.

clue.text: Seduced into being escorted round the old city

indicators.note: going round something means wrapping about it, so one piece encircles the other

parts.note: escorted means guided or led
Ur of the Chaldees, the crossword's favourite ancient city

explanation.surface: A girl is seduced after being walked round an ancient city.
explanation.definitionFit: To entice or tempt someone away with promises is to seduce them, so the past tenses match.

clue.text: My fair lady is not always so barefaced

parts.words: My fair lady is not always so
parts.note: surface: a lady is not always so shameless
setter's reading: taken literally, a bare face has no hair on it, and a fairground bearded lady does

explanation.walkthrough: Barefaced usually means shameless; read literally it means smooth-chinned, and the fairground's bearded lady is the exception.
explanation.definitionFit: A face with no hair on the chin is literally bare, so the word describes a smooth, unwhiskered face.

clue.text: Steals what belongs to the devil?

definitions.meaning: second meaning: possessive of Old Nick, a name for Satan

explanation.walkthrough: Old Nick is a traditional English name for the Devil, so his property is 'Nick's'.
explanation.definitionFit: In slang, to pinch or steal something is to nick it, and the third-person present form matches.

clue.text: Downright rascally

definitions.meaning: second meaning: roguish, the older sense of the word in '... knave'

explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means complete or utter, and it once meant notorious or roguish, as in Shakespeare's arrant knave.

clue.text: An unsurpassed performance is for the history books

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the best result yet achieved
second meaning: a written account kept for posterity

explanation.definitionFit: The best time or score ever achieved is a sporting best, and a documented account of events is preserved for history.

clue.text: Verdict which is unfavourable to the Archdeacon

parts.note: not in favour of something is to be not pro it
an archdeacon is styled the Venerable, abbreviated Ven.

explanation.surface: A court's finding goes against a senior churchman.
explanation.walkthrough: Archdeacons in the Church of England carry the title 'the Venerable', shortened to Ven. before the name.
explanation.definitionFit: Scottish law allows a third finding, besides guilty and not guilty, when evidence is insufficient to convict.

clue.text: Pinched even when seemingly under control

definitions.meaning: first meaning: stolen or grabbed, in slang
second meaning: fitted with a light horse's bit, which restrains the animal

explanation.walkthrough: A snaffle is a simple bit for a horse's mouth, so a horse so fitted is held in check.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang uses the verb for stealing or grabbing quickly, and a horse wearing the plain bit is reined in.

clue.text: Nero's pal makes the column

definitions.note: the answer is the adjective naming this column, as in the newspaper's personal column

indicators.note: makes here means is made into, so the letters before it are fashioned into something new

parts.note: taken as written: eight letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: The emperor's friend gets a mention in the newspaper column.
explanation.definitionFit: Newspapers carry a section of private small advertisements and messages known by this adjective as its column title.

clue.text: Keep Richard out from the Eisteddfod?

indicators.note: spoken out loud, so the phrase before it is judged by how it is said

parts.note: to bar is to keep out, and Dick is the pet form of Richard

explanation.surface: Welsh festival organisers try to keep a man called Richard away.
explanation.walkthrough: The parse is uncertain: 'keep out' gives BAR and Richard is Dick, and the phrase said quickly gives the answer. An Eisteddfod is a Welsh festival of poetry and song.
explanation.definitionFit: Welsh festivals celebrate poets and singers in the old tradition of bards, so their work is of the bards.

clue.text: Very strung up at the time

definitions.meaning: first meaning: nervous and on edge
second meaning: the grammatical form of a verb that shows when an action happens

explanation.definitionFit: Taut nerves make a person anxious, and grammar uses the noun for a verb's time reference such as past or present.

clue.text: Coupled with the name of Ringwood!

definitions.text: Coupled with the name of Ringwood!

parts.note: surface: someone linked by name with a place, as Ringwood is an English town
setter's reading: the hound paired with Ringwood in the hunting song D'ye ken John Peel

explanation.walkthrough: The song D'ye ken John Peel names his hounds 'Ranter and Ringwood, Bellman and True'; hounds are coupled in pairs.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cumbrian huntsman's song lists his hounds in pairs, and this one is named alongside Ringwood in the chorus.

clue.text: Underground travellers, human and vegetable?

parts.note: surface: passengers on London's Tube
setter's reading: swollen roots like potatoes, which also live below ground

explanation.walkthrough: The Tube is London's underground railway, so its riders could be called 'Tubers'; potatoes are tubers too.
explanation.definitionFit: Potatoes and similar swollen storage stems grow in soil, and the word also puns on riders of the London Tube.

clue.text: Pawnees' qualification, but not necessarily those of Oklahoma

definitions.text: Pawnees' qualification, but not necessarily those of Oklahoma

parts.words: but not necessarily those of Oklahoma
parts.note: surface: the Native American Pawnee people of Oklahoma
setter's reading: pawnees are pawnbrokers, nicknamed 'uncle', so their quality is uncle-like

explanation.walkthrough: A pawnee is the person who takes goods in pawn, and 'uncle' is old British slang for a pawnbroker.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means like an uncle, kindly and indulgent, and pawnbrokers are traditionally nicknamed uncle by their customers.

clue.text: What happened to Mrs Glasse's hare?

definitions.text: What happened to Mrs Glasse's hare?

parts.note: surface: the famous misquotation 'First catch your hare', which tempts the answer caught
setter's reading: the cookbook actually said take your hare once it has been skinned

explanation.walkthrough: Hannah Glasse's 18th-century cookery book is misquoted as 'First catch your hare'; her text says 'take your hare when it is cased', meaning skinned.
explanation.definitionFit: In old cookery, to case a hare or rabbit is to strip off its skin before roasting it.

clue.text: The immature ghost

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the young, grub stage of an insect
second meaning: the Latin word for a spectre or mask

explanation.definitionFit: Grubs and caterpillars are the juvenile stage of insects, and the Latin source word meant a spirit or spectre.

clue.text: Those little quarrels among lutanists

parts.note: surface: small disagreements between musicians
setter's reading: Tennyson's 'little rift within the lute', a small flaw that spoils the music

explanation.walkthrough: Tennyson wrote of 'the little rift within the lute, / That by and by will make the music mute', meaning a small quarrel between lovers.
explanation.definitionFit: Small breaks in friendship or disagreements are splits or cracks, as in the lines Tennyson wrote about the lute.

clue.text: "You're kidding!" as they might have said on this island

definitions.text: "You're kidding!" as they might have said on this island

parts.note: surface: an exclamation of disbelief

parts.words: as they might have said on this island
parts.note: setter's reading: the allusion is uncertain; possibly the goats kept by the marooned Ben Gunn in Stevenson's novel

explanation.walkthrough: The parse is uncertain. Stevenson's Treasure Island has Ben Gunn living on goats, and 'kidding' may refer to them giving birth to kids.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the name of the Stevenson novel's island where pirates' gold lay buried, the first word of its title.

clue.text: "She plucked that piece of geranium-flower"

parts.note: surface: a girl picking a flower
setter's reading: name the girl of Browning's poem in which this line appears

explanation.walkthrough: The line is from Robert Browning's Evelyn Hope, about a dead girl of sixteen: 'She plucked that piece of geranium-flower'.
explanation.definitionFit: Browning's poem mourns a young girl of that first name, and the quoted line describes her picking the flower.

clue.text: Ida rules out what's left

indicators.note: out as in out of order or out of place, so the letters before it are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written: eight letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Ida dismisses whatever remains on the table.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes a remainder, the part remaining after the rest has been removed or used up.

clue.text: There is something electric in seeing Gratiano dallying there

indicators.note: something inside what you are looking at is concealed within the following words

parts.note: the run of letters across the end of the name and the start of the next word

explanation.surface: Watching Gratiano flirt in The Merchant of Venice gives an electric thrill.
explanation.walkthrough: Gratiano is a character in Shakespeare's The Merchant of Venice; the answer straddles his name and the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective relates to the positive electrode of a battery or cell, so it is an electrical term.
